Asynchronous TypeScript and ES Modules

← Back to Course Package
⚠️ The Missing Extension Mystery
When importing local files in an ESM project, you must include the .js extension in your import string even if your source file is currently .ts. If you omit the extension or use .ts, the runtime will fail to locate the module, leading to 'Module not found' errors.
⚠️ The package.json 'Type' Trap
Node.js defaults to CommonJS unless you manually add "type": "module" to your package.json file. Without this property, your 'import' and 'export' statements will throw a syntax error because Node expects 'require' instead.
⚠️ The Hanging CLI
When using the readline module for user input, you must explicitly call rl.close() once the interaction is finished. If you forget to close the interface, your Node.js process will remain active and the terminal will hang indefinitely instead of returning to the prompt.
⚠️ String Math Sabotage
The readline.question() method always returns user input as a string, regardless of whether they typed a number. If you perform addition without using Number() or parseFloat(), JavaScript will perform string concatenation (e.g., "10" + "5" becomes "105") instead of mathematical addition.
⚠️ Top-Level Await Configuration
Using 'await' outside of an async function requires specific 'target' and 'module' settings like 'ESNext' in your tsconfig.json. If these are set to older versions like 'ES5' or 'CommonJS', the compiler will reject top-level await as a syntax error.
